text.title: Ivy Day in the Committee Room
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: A group of political canvassers gather in a Dublin committee room on the anniversary of Parnell's death, discussing electoral politics, morality, and Irish nationalism while waiting for payment from their candidate.

old-jack.name: Jack
old-jack.description: An old caretaker of the committee room, bony and hairy, with moist blue eyes. He tends the fire, serves drinks, and laments his son's drinking and lack of discipline.
old-jack.context: Works as caretaker in the Committee Room in Wicklow Street, Dublin

data.physicalDescription: old man's face, very bony and hairy, moist blue eyes, moist mouth

mr-oconnor.name: Mr O'Connor
mr-oconnor.description: A grey-haired young man whose face is disfigured by blotches and pimples. He is engaged as a canvasser for Tierney's election campaign. He speaks in a husky falsetto and wears an ivy leaf in his lapel.
textMentions: Mr O'Connor, a grey-haired young man
mr-oconnor.context: Canvasser for Tierney's agent in Royal Exchange Ward

data.physicalDescription: grey-haired young man, face disfigured by many blotches and pimples, wears ivy leaf in lapel

mr-hynes.name: Mr Hynes
mr-hynes.description: A tall, slender young man with a light brown moustache. He is a political activist and poet who wrote 'The Death of Parnell'. He wears an ivy leaf in his lapel and is suspected by Henchy of being a spy for Colgan.
textMentions: a tall, slender young man with a light brown moustache
mr-hynes.context: Political activist and writer, supporter of working-class representation and Parnell's memory

data.physicalDescription: tall, slender young man with light brown moustache, imminent drops of rain on hat brim, collar turned up, ivy leaf in lapel

mr-henchy.name: Mr Henchy
mr-henchy.description: A bustling little man with a snuffling nose and very cold ears. He is a pragmatic canvasser who focuses on getting votes through persuasion about economic benefits. He is suspicious of Hynes and critical of Tierney.
textMentions: a bustling little man with a snuffling nose
mr-henchy.context: Canvasser for Tierney's campaign, experienced in electoral politics

data.physicalDescription: bustling little man with snuffling nose and very cold ears

mr-tierney.name: Mr Richard J. Tierney
mr-tierney.description: The Nationalist candidate for Royal Exchange Ward. He is not present in the story but is frequently discussed. He is suspected of being dishonest and reluctant to pay his canvassers. His father kept a hand-me-down shop in Mary's Lane.
mr-tierney.context: Nationalist candidate for Royal Exchange Ward, Dublin municipal elections

mr-crofton.name: Mr Crofton
mr-crofton.description: A very fat man whose blue serge clothes seem in danger of falling from his sloping figure. He has a big face resembling a young ox's, staring blue eyes, and a grizzled moustache. He was formerly a canvasser for the Conservative candidate but switched to Tierney when the Conservatives withdrew.
mr-crofton.context: Canvasser who switched from Conservative to Nationalist candidate

data.physicalDescription: very fat man, blue serge clothes in danger of falling, big face like young ox's, staring blue eyes, grizzled moustache

mr-lyons.name: Mr Lyons
mr-lyons.description: A much younger and frailer man than Crofton, with a thin, clean-shaven face. He wears a very high double collar and a wide-brimmed bowler hat. He is argumentative about the King's address and compares Edward to Parnell.

data.physicalDescription: much younger and frailer, thin clean-shaven face, very high double collar, wide-brimmed bowler hat

father-keon.name: Father Keon
father-keon.description: A mysterious figure resembling a poor clergyman or poor actor. His black clothes are tightly buttoned on his short body. His face is shining with raindrops and has the appearance of damp yellow cheese. He has a very long mouth and very bright blue eyes. His status as a priest is unclear.
textMentions: A person resembling a poor clergyman or a poor actor
father-keon.context: Unclear ecclesiastical status, associated with Fanning, appears to be a 'black sheep' priest

data.physicalDescription: resembles poor clergyman or actor, black clothes tightly buttoned on short body, face shining with raindrops like damp yellow cheese, very long mouth, very bright blue eyes, round hat of hard black felt

boy-messenger.name: Boy
boy-messenger.description: A young messenger boy who delivers stout from the Black Eagle pub. He is seventeen years old and is given a drink by the men, which prompts the old man's comment about 'the thin edge of the wedge'.

jacks-son.name: Jack's Son
jacks-son.description: The nineteen-year-old son of old Jack. He is a chronic drinker who refuses to work steadily. Jack sent him to Christian Brothers school but he has turned out badly. He is disrespectful to his father when drunk.
jacks-son.context: Son of Jack the caretaker, chronic alcoholic

colgan.name: Colgan
colgan.description: A working-man and bricklayer who is running as a candidate, presumably against Tierney. He is defended by Hynes as a legitimate working-class representative. Henchy dismisses him as a 'tinker'.
colgan.context: Working-class candidate, bricklayer, represents labour interests

mr-fanning.name: Mr Fanning
mr-fanning.description: A man associated with the Black Eagle pub and Father Keon. He is mentioned as being at the pub and is the subject of Father Keon's visit. He appears to have some control over the distribution of stout.
mr-fanning.context: Associated with Black Eagle pub, involved in electoral politics

grimes.name: Grimes
grimes.description: A voter in Aungier Street whom O'Connor canvassed. He was non-committal about his vote but O'Connor believes he will vote for Tierney because Father Burke's name was mentioned.
grimes.context: Voter in Aungier Street, Royal Exchange Ward

father-burke.name: Father Burke
father-burke.description: A priest whose name is mentioned by O'Connor as a nominator for Tierney. His endorsement appears to influence voters.

parkes.name: Parkes
parkes.description: A voter whom Henchy successfully canvassed and secured a vote from.

atkinson.name: Atkinson
atkinson.description: A voter whom Henchy successfully canvassed and secured a vote from.

ward.name: Ward
ward.description: A voter from Dawson Street whom Henchy successfully canvassed. He is described as a fine old chap, a regular old toff, and an old Conservative. Henchy persuaded him by arguing that Tierney is a respectable man and big ratepayer.
ward.context: Voter in Dawson Street, Royal Exchange Ward, Conservative sympathizer

data.physicalDescription: fine old chap, regular old toff, old Conservative

parnell.name: Charles Stewart Parnell
parnell.description: The deceased Irish nationalist leader whose death is commemorated on October 6th. He is frequently referenced throughout the story as a symbol of Irish nationalism and integrity. Hynes' poem celebrates his memory.
parnell.context: Irish nationalist leader, died October 6, 1891, symbol of Irish independence

king-edward.name: King Edward VII
king-edward.description: The British monarch whose potential visit to Dublin is the subject of debate. Henchy argues for welcoming him as good for business; Lyons and others oppose the address of welcome as contrary to Irish nationalist principles.
king-edward.context: British monarch, potential visitor to Dublin

major-sirr.name: Major Sirr
major-sirr.description: A historical figure referenced by Henchy as a comparison to a contemporary 'patriot' with a cock-eye. Sirr is invoked as a symbol of betrayal of Irish interests.
major-sirr.context: Historical figure associated with betrayal of Irish causes

larry-hynes.name: Larry Hynes
larry-hynes.description: The deceased father of Joe Hynes. Henchy speaks of him as a decent respectable man who did many good turns in his day.

keegan.name: Keegan
keegan.description: A porter who works for the current Lord Mayor. The old man recounts Keegan's story about the Lord Mayor's frugal dinner of a pound of chops.

alderman-cowley.name: Alderman Cowley
alderman-cowley.description: An alderman whom Tierney (the 'little shoeboy') is seen talking to at the counter of the Black Eagle pub. He appears to be involved in some political dealing.
alderman-cowley.context: Alderman in Dublin, involved in electoral politics

committee-room-wicklow-st.name: Committee Room in Wicklow Street
committee-room-wicklow-st.description: A denuded room with bare walls except for a copy of an election address. It contains a small table heaped with papers, a fireplace with a mantelpiece, and candlesticks. The room is cold and dark, lit by fire and candles.
committee-room-wicklow-st.context: Headquarters for Tierney's electoral campaign in Royal Exchange Ward

royal-exchange-ward.name: Royal Exchange Ward
royal-exchange-ward.description: A ward in Dublin where the municipal election is taking place. It includes streets like Aungier Street, Dawson Street, and Suffolk Street.
royal-exchange-ward.context: Electoral district in Dublin for municipal elections

black-eagle-pub.name: The Black Eagle
black-eagle-pub.description: A public house where stout is obtained. Fanning is located there, and the boy messenger comes from there with bottles of stout.

aungier-street.name: Aungier Street
aungier-street.description: A street in Dublin where O'Connor canvassed voters, including Grimes.

dawson-street.name: Dawson Street
dawson-street.description: A street in Dublin where Henchy and Crofton canvassed and secured votes from Ward and others.

suffolk-street.name: Suffolk Street
suffolk-street.description: A street in Dublin where O'Connor observed Tierney, Fanning, and Alderman Cowley together.

marys-lane.name: Mary's Lane
marys-lane.description: A lane in Dublin where Tierney's father kept a hand-me-down shop. Men used to go there on Sunday mornings before houses were open to buy waistcoats or trousers.

mansion-house.name: Mansion House
mansion-house.description: The official residence of the Lord Mayor of Dublin. Referenced in discussion of the Lord Mayor's frugal lifestyle.
textMentions: Driving out of the Mansion House
mansion-house.context: Official residence of Lord Mayor of Dublin

kavanaghs.name: Kavanagh's
kavanaghs.description: A place where Fanning and Father Keon are often seen together, mentioned in discussion of Keon's mysterious nature.

dublin.name: Dublin
dublin.description: The city where the entire story takes place. It is the setting for electoral politics, nationalist sentiment, and the commemoration of Parnell.
dublin.context: Capital of Ireland, center of nationalist politics

cardboard-piece.name: Piece of Cardboard
cardboard-piece.description: A piece of cardboard used by Jack to rake cinders and spread them over the coals, and later to fan the fire.

tobacco-cigarette.name: Tobacco
tobacco-cigarette.description: Tobacco that O'Connor rolls into a cigarette. He shapes it into a cylinder and licks the paper to seal it.

election-card.name: Election Card
election-card.description: A pasteboard card printed with Tierney's election address soliciting votes and influence for the Royal Exchange Ward election. O'Connor tears a strip off one to light his cigarette.
textMentions: a pack of thin pasteboard cards
election-card.physicalDescription: thin pasteboard card with printed text

ivy-leaf.name: Ivy Leaf
ivy-leaf.description: A dark glossy ivy leaf worn in the lapel of O'Connor's coat and later in Hynes' coat. It is a symbol of Parnell's memory, as October 6th is Ivy Day, the anniversary of Parnell's death.
textMentions: a leaf of dark glossy ivy
ivy-leaf.context: Symbol of Parnell's memory on Ivy Day

candlesticks.name: Candlesticks
candlesticks.description: Two candlesticks that Jack retrieves from the room and thrusts into the fire to light them, then carries to the table to illuminate the room.
candlesticks.context: Used for lighting the committee room

election-address.name: Election Address
election-address.description: A copy of an election address posted on the wall of the committee room. It is the only decoration in the bare room.
textMentions: a copy of an election address
election-address.context: Campaign material displayed in committee room

stout-bottles.name: Bottles of Stout
stout-bottles.description: Bottles of stout delivered from the Black Eagle pub. The men drink from them throughout the evening. They are opened using a corkscrew or by heating on the fire hob.
stout-bottles.context: Alcoholic beverage consumed during the gathering

basket.name: Basket
basket.description: A basket used by the boy messenger to deliver the bottles of stout from the Black Eagle pub.

corkscrew.name: Corkscrew
corkscrew.description: A corkscrew borrowed from O'Farrell's to open the bottles of stout. It is used to open several bottles before being returned.

cigarette-papers.name: Cigarette Papers
cigarette-papers.description: Papers used by O'Connor to roll cigarettes. He takes them out to hide his emotion after Hynes' recitation.

hat.name: Hat
hat.description: Hynes' hat, which he removes and lays on the table before standing to recite his poem.

tierney-campaign.name: Tierney's Campaign
tierney-campaign.description: The electoral campaign for Mr Richard J. Tierney, the Nationalist candidate for Royal Exchange Ward. The campaign employs canvassers including O'Connor, Henchy, Crofton, and Lyons.
tierney-campaign.historicalContext: Dublin municipal elections in post-Parnell era
tierney-campaign.organizationalStructure: Candidate with agent, canvassers, and committee room

colgan-campaign.name: Colgan's Campaign
colgan-campaign.description: The electoral campaign for Colgan, a working-man and bricklayer candidate. He is defended by Hynes as a legitimate working-class representative.

conservative-party.name: Conservative Party
conservative-party.description: The Conservative political party in Dublin. They initially had a candidate but withdrew and gave their support to the Nationalist candidate Tierney.

e01.description: Old Jack rakes cinders together with a piece of cardboard and spreads them judiciously over the whitening dome of coals.

e02.description: Mr O'Connor, a grey-haired young man with a disfigured face, has just brought tobacco into a shapely cylinder but when spoken to he undoes his handiwork meditatively.

e03.description: Mr O'Connor tears a strip off an election card and, lighting it, lights his cigarette. The flame lights up a dark glossy ivy leaf in his lapel.

e04.description: Jack begins to lament his son's behavior, saying it's hard to know what way to bring up children and that his son has turned out badly despite being sent to Christian Brothers.

e05.description: Jack continues his lament, saying he would beat his son if he were younger, and blames the mother for coddling him.

e06.description: Jack reveals his son is nineteen years old and refuses to work steadily, drinking away any wages he earns.

e07.description: Mr Hynes enters the dark committee room, asking what they are doing in the dark.

e08.description: The old man leaves the hearth and returns with two candlesticks which he thrusts into the fire and carries to the table.

e09.description: The candlelight reveals a denuded room with bare walls except for a copy of an election address, a small table heaped with papers, and the fire losing its cheerful colour.

e10.description: Mr Hynes asks if Tierney has paid them yet. O'Connor expresses hope that Tierney will not leave them in the lurch.

e11.description: Hynes laughs and assures them Tierney will pay. O'Connor hopes he'll look smart about it.

e12.description: Hynes defends Colgan as a working-man and bricklayer, arguing that working-men have as good a right to be in the Corporation as anyone else, and better than 'shoneens'.

e13.description: Hynes argues that the working-man gets all kicks and no halfpence, and that labour produces everything. He criticizes Tierney for only wanting to get a job.

e14.description: Hynes criticizes the proposed address of welcome to King Edward, asking why they should kowtow to a foreign king.

e15.description: O'Connor notes that Tierney goes in on the Nationalist ticket and won't vote for the address. Hynes expresses doubt, calling Tierney 'Tricky Dicky Tierney'.

e16.description: Hynes points to the ivy leaf in his lapel, saying 'If this man was alive,' referring to Parnell.

e17.description: O'Connor agrees, and the old man nostalgically says 'Musha, God be with them times! There was some life in it then.'

e18.description: Hynes leaves the room, saying 'It'll be all right when King Eddie comes' and 'I'm off for the present.'

e19.description: Henchy asks what brings Hynes to the committee room and what he wants.

e20.description: Henchy expresses his private opinion that Hynes is a spy for Colgan, sent to find out how they're getting on.

e21.description: Henchy admits Hynes' father was a decent man but expresses doubt about Hynes himself, saying he can't understand a fellow sponging.

e22.description: Henchy reveals that Tierney's father kept a hand-me-down shop in Mary's Lane, where men used to go on Sunday mornings to buy waistcoats or trousers.

e23.description: Henchy adds that Tierney's father always had a tricky little black bottle in a corner, suggesting Tierney's origins in dishonesty.

e24.description: Father Keon appears at the door, resembling a poor clergyman or actor, with black clothes and a face shining with raindrops.

e25.description: Henchy greets Father Keon and invites him to sit, but Keon quickly declines, saying he's just looking for Mr Fanning.

e26.description: Henchy tells Keon that Fanning is at the Black Eagle pub and offers to light him downstairs.

e27.description: O'Connor asks Henchy what Father Keon is exactly. Henchy says he's a 'black sheep' priest, an unfortunate man of some kind.

e28.description: O'Connor asks how Keon makes a living. Henchy says it's a mystery and that Keon is travelling on his own account.

e29.description: O'Connor observes that Tierney, Fanning, and Alderman Cowley were seen together at Suffolk Street corner, suggesting some political dealing.

e30.description: A boy arrives at the door with a basket of bottles from the Black Eagle pub.

e31.description: Henchy sends the boy to O'Farrell's to borrow a corkscrew, saying they won't keep it a minute.

e32.description: The boy returns with the corkscrew. The old man opens three bottles and is handing back the corkscrew when Henchy asks if the boy would like a drink.

e33.description: The old man reluctantly opens another bottle for the boy, who is seventeen years old. The boy drinks and leaves.

e34.description: The old man tells a story about Keegan, the porter, who said the current Lord Mayor sent out for only a pound of chops for his dinner.

e35.description: The old man expresses amazement at the Lord Mayor's frugality, saying 'what kind of people is going at all now?'

e36.description: Two men enter the room: Crofton, a very fat man, and Lyons, a much younger and frailer man.

e37.description: Henchy takes two bottles from the table and puts them on the hob of the fire to open them by heating.

e38.description: Henchy reports that he and Crofton got votes from Parkes, Atkinson, and Ward of Dawson Street, describing his persuasion tactics.

e39.description: Henchy describes how he persuaded Ward by arguing that Tierney is respectable and a big ratepayer with extensive property.

e40.description: Lyons asks about the address to the King. Henchy argues that the King's coming will mean an influx of money into the country.

e41.description: O'Connor questions why they should welcome the King of England, invoking Parnell. Henchy argues that Parnell is dead and the King is a decent fellow.

e42.description: Henchy describes the King as an ordinary knockabout fellow who is fond of his glass of grog and a good sportsman.

e43.description: Lyons argues that they have ideals and compares Edward to Parnell, questioning why they would welcome Edward after what Parnell did.

e44.description: O'Connor notes that it is Parnell's anniversary and suggests they not stir up bad blood. He notes that even Conservatives respect Parnell now that he's dead.

e45.description: Crofton speaks in a deep voice, saying 'Our side of the house respects him, because he was a gentleman.'

e46.description: Henchy catches sight of Hynes in the doorway and calls out 'Come in, Joe! Come in!'

e47.description: O'Connor asks Hynes to recite the poem he wrote. Henchy enthusiastically encourages him, calling it a splendid thing.

e48.description: Hynes hesitates, then removes his hat, lays it on the table, and stands up. After a pause, he announces 'THE DEATH OF PARNELL' and recites the poem.

e49.description: After Hynes finishes reciting, there is silence followed by a burst of clapping, even from Lyons. All the auditors drink from their bottles in silence.

rel-jack-oconnor.name: Jack and O'Connor
rel-jack-oconnor.description: Jack and O'Connor sit together by the fire in the committee room, having spent much of the day there due to inclement weather. They have a comfortable, familiar relationship.

rel-jack-hynes.name: Jack and Hynes
rel-jack-hynes.description: Jack and Hynes interact politely but with some distance. Jack is skeptical of Hynes and doesn't give him a warm welcome.

rel-oconnor-hynes.name: O'Connor and Hynes
rel-oconnor-hynes.description: O'Connor and Hynes have a friendly relationship. O'Connor defends Hynes against Henchy's suspicions, calling him 'a decent skin' and 'a straight man'.

rel-henchy-oconnor.name: Henchy and O'Connor
rel-henchy-oconnor.description: Henchy and O'Connor work together as canvassers. Henchy is more cynical and talkative, while O'Connor is more thoughtful and sympathetic.

rel-henchy-hynes.name: Henchy and Hynes
rel-henchy-hynes.description: Henchy is suspicious of Hynes, believing him to be a spy for Colgan. However, he later admits Hynes is 'a stroke above' the Castle hacks and praises him for sticking to Parnell.

rel-henchy-crofton.name: Henchy and Crofton
rel-henchy-crofton.description: Henchy and Crofton work together as canvassers. Crofton is silent and aloof, considering his companions beneath him.

rel-crofton-lyons.name: Crofton and Lyons
rel-crofton-lyons.description: Crofton and Lyons are canvassers who work together. Lyons is argumentative and idealistic, while Crofton is silent and aloof.

rel-jack-son.name: Jack and His Son
rel-jack-son.description: Jack is deeply troubled by his son's drinking and lack of discipline. He sent his son to Christian Brothers school but the son has turned out badly. Jack would beat him if he were younger.

rel-henchy-tierney.name: Henchy and Tierney
rel-henchy-tierney.description: Henchy works for Tierney as a canvasser but is critical of him, calling him 'Tricky Dicky' and expressing frustration about payment.

rel-oconnor-tierney.name: O'Connor and Tierney
rel-oconnor-tierney.description: O'Connor is engaged as a canvasser for Tierney's campaign. He expresses hope that Tierney will pay them.

rel-crofton-tierney.name: Crofton and Tierney
rel-crofton-tierney.description: Crofton was formerly a canvasser for the Conservative candidate but switched to Tierney when the Conservatives withdrew.

rel-lyons-tierney.name: Lyons and Tierney
rel-lyons-tierney.description: Lyons is a canvasser for Tierney's campaign. He is argumentative about the King's address and questions Tierney's commitment to nationalist principles.

rel-henchy-fanning.name: Henchy and Fanning
rel-henchy-fanning.description: Henchy is frustrated with Fanning, who is associated with Tierney and appears to have some control over the distribution of stout.

rel-hynes-parnell.name: Hynes and Parnell
rel-hynes-parnell.description: Hynes is deeply devoted to Parnell's memory. He wears an ivy leaf in his lapel on Parnell's anniversary and has written a poem celebrating Parnell's legacy.

rel-oconnor-parnell.name: O'Connor and Parnell
rel-oconnor-parnell.description: O'Connor respects Parnell's memory and wears an ivy leaf in his lapel. He is moved by Hynes' poem about Parnell.

rel-crofton-parnell.name: Crofton and Parnell
rel-crofton-parnell.description: Crofton respects Parnell as a gentleman, even though he is a Conservative. He acknowledges that Parnell was the only man who could keep order.

grp-committee-room-gathering.name: Committee Room Gathering
grp-committee-room-gathering.description: The group of men gathered in the committee room: Jack, O'Connor, Hynes, Henchy, Crofton, and Lyons. They are united by their work as canvassers for Tierney's campaign and their shared commemoration of Parnell.

grp-canvassers.name: Tierney's Canvassers
grp-canvassers.description: The group of canvassers working for Tierney's electoral campaign: O'Connor, Henchy, Crofton, and Lyons.

abs-payment-from-tierney.name: Payment from Tierney
abs-payment-from-tierney.description: The canvassers are waiting for payment from Tierney for their electoral work. This is a pressing concern throughout the evening.
abs-payment-from-tierney.origin: O'Connor expresses hope that Tierney will not leave them in the lurch

abs-parnell-memory.name: Parnell's Memory
abs-parnell-memory.description: The commemoration of Parnell's death on October 6th. The ivy leaf is a symbol of this remembrance, and Hynes' poem celebrates Parnell's legacy.
abs-parnell-memory.origin: October 6th is Ivy Day, the anniversary of Parnell's death

abs-irish-nationalism.name: Irish Nationalism
abs-irish-nationalism.description: The broader concern with Irish nationalist principles and resistance to foreign domination, particularly regarding the proposed address of welcome to King Edward.
abs-irish-nationalism.origin: Hynes criticizes the proposed address of welcome to King Edward as contrary to Irish interests

abs-working-class-representation.name: Working-Class Representation
abs-working-class-representation.description: The desire for working-class representation in electoral politics, championed by Hynes in defense of Colgan.
abs-working-class-representation.origin: Hynes argues that working-men have as good a right to be in the Corporation as anyone else

abs-jacks-son-reform.name: Jack's Son's Reform
abs-jacks-son-reform.description: Jack's desire for his son to reform and become a decent, hardworking person. This is a source of deep concern and disappointment.
abs-jacks-son-reform.origin: Jack laments his son's drinking and lack of discipline despite sending him to Christian Brothers

abs-economic-benefit.name: Economic Benefit
abs-economic-benefit.description: Henchy's pragmatic focus on the economic benefits of the King's visit and Tierney's candidacy as a ratepayer.
abs-economic-benefit.origin: Henchy argues that the King's coming will mean an influx of money into the country

mc-jack-son-failure.name: Jack's Belief in His Son's Failure
mc-jack-son-failure.description: Jack's belief that his son has turned out badly despite his efforts to raise him properly.

data.content: My son has turned out badly despite my efforts to raise him properly. I sent him to Christian Brothers and did what I could, but he drinks and is disrespectful.

mc-henchy-hynes-spy.name: Henchy's Suspicion of Hynes
mc-henchy-hynes-spy.description: Henchy's belief that Hynes is a spy for Colgan, sent to find out how Tierney's campaign is progressing.
mc-henchy-hynes-spy.subject: mr-hynes

data.content: Hynes is a spy for Colgan, sent to find out how we're getting on. He's hard up and sponging off us.

mc-oconnor-hynes-decent.name: O'Connor's Belief in Hynes' Decency

mc-oconnor-hynes-decent.subject: mr-hynes

data.content: Joe Hynes is a decent skin and a straight man. He's clever with the pen and stuck to Parnell.

mc-henchy-tierney-dishonest.name: Henchy's Belief in Tierney's Dishonesty
mc-henchy-tierney-dishonest.description: Henchy's belief that Tierney is dishonest and evasive, based on his family background and behavior.
mc-henchy-tierney-dishonest.subject: mr-tierney

data.content: Tierney is dishonest and evasive. His father kept a hand-me-down shop and had a tricky black bottle. He's 'Tricky Dicky' and won't pay us.

mc-hynes-parnell-greatness.name: Hynes' Belief in Parnell's Greatness
mc-hynes-parnell-greatness.description: Hynes' belief that Parnell was a great leader and uncrowned king who was betrayed by cowards.
mc-hynes-parnell-greatness.subject: parnell

data.content: Parnell was our Uncrowned King, a great leader who was betrayed by coward hounds and fawning priests. His memory should be honored.

mc-henchy-king-decent.name: Henchy's Belief in the King's Decency

mc-lyons-ideals-matter.name: Lyons' Belief in Ideals
mc-lyons-ideals-matter.description: Lyons' belief that Irish ideals and Parnell's legacy should take precedence over economic pragmatism.
mc-lyons-ideals-matter.subject: parnell

data.content: We have our ideals. Parnell was a fit man to lead us, and we should not welcome a man like Edward after what he did.

mc-crofton-parnell-gentleman.name: Crofton's Belief in Parnell's Gentlemanliness
mc-crofton-parnell-gentleman.description: Crofton's belief that Parnell was a gentleman and deserves respect.
mc-crofton-parnell-gentleman.subject: parnell

data.content: Parnell was a gentleman. Our side of the house respects him because he was a gentleman.

mc-jack-mother-spoils-son.name: Jack's Belief About His Wife
mc-jack-mother-spoils-son.description: Jack's belief that his wife coddles and spoils their son, contributing to his bad behavior.
mc-jack-mother-spoils-son.subject: jacks-son

data.content: The mother cocks him up with this and that. She spoils him, which is what ruins children.

mc-henchy-working-class-representation.name: Henchy's Skepticism of Working-Class Representation

Formalist Reading.name: Formalist Reading
Formalist Reading.description: A formalist interpretation focusing on narrative structure, literary devices, symbolism, and the formal properties of the text itself. This reading emphasizes how Joyce uses form, language, imagery, and structural patterns to create meaning independent of historical or biographical context.

theme-paralysis.name: Paralysis and Inaction
theme-paralysis.description: The formal structure traps characters in circular dialogue and waiting. The story begins and ends in the same room with minimal external action, creating a sense of stasis. Characters discuss ideals (Parnell, nationalism, working-class representation) but take no meaningful action, embodying the paralysis of Dublin society.

theme-corruption-of-ideals.name: Corruption and Degradation of Ideals
theme-corruption-of-ideals.description: The formal contrast between elevated ideals (Parnell, nationalism, working-class dignity) and the sordid reality of electoral politics creates ironic tension. Language shifts from noble rhetoric to petty gossip and mercenary concerns, formally enacting the corruption of principles.

theme-memory-vs-present.name: Memory Versus Present Reality
theme-memory-vs-present.description: The formal structure juxtaposes nostalgic references to Parnell (past) with the shabby present of the committee room. The ivy leaf symbolizes this temporal split. The poem at the end formally resurrects the past, only to be followed by silence and drinking—the past cannot sustain the present.

theme-language-and-authenticity.name: Language, Rhetoric, and Authenticity
theme-language-and-authenticity.description: The text formally explores how language obscures truth. Characters use rhetoric to persuade voters, gossip to undermine rivals, and formal poetry to commemorate the dead. The gap between what is said and what is true creates formal irony throughout.

sym-ivy-leaf.name: Ivy Leaf
sym-ivy-leaf.description: A formal symbol of Parnell's memory and Irish nationalism. Its appearance in lapels creates visual continuity and marks characters' allegiances. The leaf is dark, glossy, and artificial—a preserved memorial rather than living growth, formally embodying the deadness of the nationalist ideal in the present.

sym-committee-room.name: The Committee Room
sym-committee-room.description: A formally enclosed space that structures the entire narrative. The bare walls, denuded furnishings, and cold fire create a formally austere setting that mirrors the emptiness of the political enterprise. The room's darkness and need for candlelight formally suggest obscurity and moral dimness.

sym-fire-and-light.name: Fire and Light
sym-fire-and-light.description: Formally contrasts illumination with obscurity. The fire begins cheerful but loses color; candlelight reveals a denuded room. Light formally fails to clarify or inspire—it merely exposes emptiness. The heating of bottles on the fire transforms a symbol of warmth into a means of obtaining alcohol.

currentMeanings.description: Warmth corrupted into servitude to appetite

sym-stout-bottles.name: Stout Bottles
sym-stout-bottles.description: Formally represent the substitution of material comfort for ideological substance. The bottles arrive as a gift but must be opened, requiring borrowed tools. They are heated, drunk in silence, and offered to a boy—formally enacting the corruption and dissipation of resources and principles.

currentMeanings.description: Substitution of drink for political action

sym-poem.name: Hynes' Poem
sym-poem.description: Formally the climax and resolution of the narrative. Its recitation creates the only moment of unified emotional response, yet it is immediately followed by silence and drinking. The poem formally demonstrates how language can move an audience while changing nothing material—it is a formal gesture that cannot sustain itself.

currentMeanings.description: Resurrection and immediate death of ideals

symrel-ivy-nationalism.name: Ivy Leaf as Nationalist Symbol
symrel-ivy-nationalism.description: The ivy leaf formally embodies the theme of memory versus present reality. Its artificial preservation mirrors the formal structure of the story itself—a contained, artificial space where the past is commemorated but cannot be revived.
symrel-ivy-nationalism.nature: The leaf is a formal marker of temporal disjunction, worn by characters who speak of Parnell but cannot act on his legacy.
symrel-ivy-nationalism.interpretation: The leaf is a formal marker of temporal disjunction, worn by characters who speak of Parnell but cannot act on his legacy.

symrel-room-paralysis.name: Committee Room as Formal Enclosure
symrel-room-paralysis.description: The room's structure formally enacts paralysis. Characters enter and exit but the room remains unchanged. The bare walls and minimal furnishings formally represent the emptiness of political discourse.
symrel-room-paralysis.nature: The room is a formal container that prevents action and change, mirroring the circular structure of the dialogue.
symrel-room-paralysis.interpretation: The room is a formal container that prevents action and change, mirroring the circular structure of the dialogue.

symrel-stout-corruption.name: Stout as Corruption of Ideals
symrel-stout-corruption.description: The bottles formally replace ideological substance with material consumption. Their arrival marks the shift from political debate to drinking, formally enacting the corruption theme.
symrel-stout-corruption.nature: The stout formally substitutes for action and principle, offered even to a boy, spreading corruption downward through generations.
symrel-stout-corruption.interpretation: The stout formally substitutes for action and principle, offered even to a boy, spreading corruption downward through generations.

symrel-poem-language.name: Poem as Language and Authenticity
symrel-poem-language.description: The poem formally demonstrates the power and limitation of language. It moves the audience emotionally but changes nothing materially, formally illustrating the gap between rhetoric and reality.
symrel-poem-language.nature: The poem is the most authentic moment in the story, yet it is immediately followed by silence and drinking, formally showing how language cannot sustain ideals.
symrel-poem-language.interpretation: The poem is the most authentic moment in the story, yet it is immediately followed by silence and drinking, formally showing how language cannot sustain ideals.

narrator.name: Third-Person Limited Narrator
narrator.description: The narrator maintains formal distance from characters while occasionally entering their consciousness. The narrative voice is detached and ironic, formally emphasizing the gap between characters' self-perception and reality. The narrator's descriptions are precise and visual, focusing on physical details and formal properties of the scene.

reader.name: Implied Reader
reader.description: The formalist reader attends to narrative structure, symbolism, and linguistic patterns. This reader recognizes the circular structure, the ironic contrasts, and the formal properties that create meaning. The reader is positioned to see the gap between what characters say and what the formal structure reveals.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: Joyce as a formalist craftsman constructing a narrative that embodies its themes through structure, symbol, and language. The author uses formal properties—enclosure, circularity, irony, contrast—to create meaning independent of plot or character psychology.

e01.note: Establishes the formal setting and introduces the fire as a symbol. The action of raking and spreading cinders formally begins the narrative's concern with containment and arrangement.

e02.note: O'Connor's undoing of his handiwork formally introduces the theme of futility and the gap between intention and action.

e03.note: The ivy leaf's first appearance is formally crucial. The flame lighting the leaf creates a symbolic moment linking fire, light, and nationalist memory.

e04.note: Jack's lament formally introduces the theme of generational corruption and the failure of education and discipline.

e05.note: Continuation of Jack's complaint, formally establishing his character as nostalgic for a past order.

e06.note: Revelation of the son's drinking formally parallels the later consumption of stout, creating a pattern of corruption.

e07.note: Hynes' entrance formally marks the introduction of the ideological voice. His question about darkness is formally ironic given the moral obscurity of the room.

e08.note: The lighting of candles is formally significant as an attempt to illuminate, yet the revelation shows only emptiness.

e09.note: The formal revelation of the denuded room is crucial. The description of bare walls and dying fire formally embodies the emptiness of the political enterprise.

e10.note: The question about payment formally introduces the material concern that will undercut ideological discussion throughout.

e11.note: Hynes' assurance about payment is formally ironic given the later revelation of non-payment.

e12.note: Hynes' defense of Colgan formally introduces the ideological debate. His use of the term 'shoneens' formally marks class consciousness and nationalist rhetoric.

e13.note: Hynes' critique of labour exploitation formally articulates the ideological position that will be undermined by the story's formal structure.

e14.note: Hynes' criticism of the King's address formally introduces the central political conflict and the tension between nationalism and pragmatism.

e15.note: O'Connor's doubt about Tierney and Hynes' skepticism formally establish the theme of corruption and untrustworthiness in politics.

e16.note: Hynes' pointing to the ivy leaf and reference to Parnell is formally the story's central symbolic moment, linking past and present.

e17.note: Jack's nostalgic response formally establishes the theme of memory versus present reality. His phrase 'there was some life in it then' formally contrasts past vitality with present emptiness.

e18.note: Hynes' departure is formally significant as it marks the first exit of the ideological voice. His ironic comment about King Eddie formally undercuts his own position.

e19.note: Henchy's question about Hynes formally introduces suspicion and gossip, shifting the narrative tone.

e20.note: Henchy's accusation that Hynes is a spy formally introduces the theme of corruption and untrustworthiness. The accusation itself is unsubstantiated, formally showing how gossip replaces knowledge.

e21.note: Henchy's criticism of Hynes formally contrasts his father's respectability with his own questionable character, establishing a pattern of generational decline.

e22.note: The revelation of Tierney's father's hand-me-down shop formally establishes Tierney's origins in commerce and suggests dishonesty.

e23.note: The 'tricky little black bottle' formally symbolizes Tierney's dishonest origins. The bottle is a formal echo of the stout bottles that will later appear.

e24.note: Father Keon's appearance is formally significant as an intrusion of religious authority into the secular political space. His description as resembling a 'poor clergyman or actor' formally suggests ambiguity.

e25.note: Keon's quick refusal to sit formally marks him as an outsider and transient figure.

e26.note: Henchy's direction to the Black Eagle pub formally connects Keon to the source of the stout that will later arrive.

e27.note: Henchy's description of Keon as a 'black sheep' priest formally introduces the theme of corruption within institutions.

e28.note: The mystery of Keon's livelihood formally establishes him as a figure of ambiguity and marginality.

e29.note: O'Connor's observation of political dealing formally suggests hidden corruption and backroom negotiations.

e30.note: The arrival of the stout bottles is formally significant as a turning point. The bottles represent material substitution for ideological substance.

e31.note: The need to borrow a corkscrew formally shows dependence and the improvised nature of the gathering.

e32.note: The opening of bottles and offer to the boy formally marks the beginning of consumption and corruption.

e33.note: The boy's drinking is formally significant as it shows the corruption spreading to youth. The old man's reluctance formally shows awareness of wrongdoing.

e34.note: Jack's story about the Lord Mayor's frugality formally introduces a note of social commentary and nostalgia for different values.

e35.note: Jack's question 'what kind of people is going at all now?' formally expresses the theme of generational decline.

e36.note: The arrival of Crofton and Lyons formally marks the gathering of all the canvassers. Crofton's description as 'very fat' formally contrasts with Lyons' frailty.

e37.note: The heating of bottles on the fire formally transforms the fire from a symbol of warmth into a means of obtaining alcohol.

e38.note: Henchy's report of canvassing success formally demonstrates the rhetoric of persuasion. His detailed account shows how voters are manipulated through appeals to respectability and economic interest.

e39.note: Henchy's description of Tierney as 'respectable' and a 'big ratepayer' formally shows how economic status substitutes for moral character.

e40.note: Lyons' question about the King's address formally reopens the ideological debate. His argument about economic benefit formally shows pragmatism overcoming principle.

e41.note: O'Connor's invocation of Parnell formally marks the return of the nationalist ideal. Henchy's response that 'Parnell is dead' formally states the theme of memory versus present reality.

e42.note: Henchy's description of the King as an 'ordinary knockabout fellow' formally reduces monarchy to ordinariness, undermining both nationalist and monarchist positions.

e43.note: Lyons' comparison of Edward to Parnell formally articulates the ideological position. His question 'why would we welcome Edward after what Parnell did?' formally shows the logical contradiction in the canvassers' position.

e44.note: O'Connor's suggestion not to stir up bad blood formally shows the desire to avoid conflict. His observation that 'even Conservatives respect Parnell now that he's dead' formally shows how death neutralizes political conflict.

e45.note: Crofton's statement that Parnell 'was a gentleman' formally shows how class respectability transcends political ideology. His voice is described as 'deep,' formally giving weight to his statement.

e46.note: Henchy's call to Hynes formally marks the return of the ideological voice. The exclamation 'Come in, Joe! Come in!' formally invites the poem that will be the story's climax.

e47.note: The request for the poem is formally significant as it marks the transition to the climactic moment. Henchy's enthusiasm formally shows the power of artistic expression.

e48.note: The recitation of the poem is formally the story's climax. Hynes' removal of his hat and formal stance create a ceremonial moment. The poem itself is the only extended passage of elevated language in the story, formally contrasting with the surrounding prose.

e49.note: The applause and silence that follow the poem are formally significant. The burst of clapping shows emotional response, yet the immediate return to drinking formally shows how the moment cannot sustain itself. The silence is formally eloquent—the poem has moved the audience but changed nothing.

old-jack.note: Jack formally represents the past and tradition. His laments about his son and nostalgia for Parnell's time formally embody the theme of generational decline and memory.

mr-oconnor.note: O'Connor formally represents the sympathetic idealist caught between principle and pragmatism. His disfigured face formally suggests moral and physical damage. His wearing of the ivy leaf formally marks his nationalist sentiment.

mr-hynes.note: Hynes formally represents the ideological voice and artistic expression. His poem is the story's formal climax. His suspicion by Henchy formally shows how idealism is viewed with distrust in the pragmatic world.

mr-henchy.note: Henchy formally represents pragmatism and corruption. His detailed accounts of persuasion formally demonstrate how rhetoric substitutes for principle. His suspicion of Hynes formally shows the conflict between idealism and pragmatism.

mr-tierney.note: Tierney, though absent, is formally significant as the object of the canvassers' efforts. His absence formally emphasizes the emptiness of the political enterprise. His dishonest origins formally establish the corruption of the political system.

mr-crofton.note: Crofton formally represents the pragmatic conservative who switches sides. His statement about Parnell being a 'gentleman' formally shows how class transcends ideology.

mr-lyons.note: Lyons formally represents youthful idealism. His arguments about the King's address formally articulate the logical contradictions in the canvassers' position.

father-keon.note: Keon formally represents ambiguity and marginality. His mysterious nature and quick departure formally suggest the corruption of religious authority.

boy-messenger.note: The boy formally represents youth corrupted by the adults. His drinking formally shows how corruption spreads downward through generations.

jacks-son.note: Jack's son, though absent, is formally significant as a symbol of generational failure. His drinking formally parallels the later consumption of stout.

colgan.note: Colgan, though absent, is formally significant as the ideological alternative to Tierney. His absence formally emphasizes the victory of pragmatism over principle.

mr-fanning.note: Fanning formally represents the connection between politics and commerce (the pub). His absence formally suggests hidden dealings.

parnell.note: Parnell, though dead, is formally the story's central figure. His memory is invoked repeatedly and formally structures the narrative. The ivy leaf and the poem formally commemorate him. His absence formally embodies the theme of memory versus present reality.

king-edward.note: The King, though absent, is formally significant as the object of political debate. His potential visit formally represents the conflict between nationalism and pragmatism.

committee-room-wicklow-st.note: The room is formally the story's central location. Its bare walls and denuded furnishings formally embody the emptiness of the political enterprise. The room's enclosure formally creates the story's circular structure.

stout-bottles.note: The bottles formally represent material substitution for ideological substance. Their arrival marks a formal turning point. Their consumption formally enacts the corruption of ideals.

ivy-leaf.note: The ivy leaf is formally the story's central symbol. Its appearance in lapels formally marks nationalist sentiment. Its artificial nature formally suggests the deadness of the ideal.

election-card.note: The card is formally torn to light a cigarette, formally showing how political rhetoric is consumed and destroyed.

candlesticks.note: The candlesticks formally represent the attempt to illuminate. Their revelation of emptiness formally shows how light fails to clarify.

abs-payment-from-tierney.note: The absent payment formally structures the canvassers' anxiety. The expectation of payment that never arrives formally embodies the theme of unfulfilled promises and corruption.

abs-parnell-memory.note: Parnell's memory is formally the story's central absence. His death is commemorated but his ideals cannot be revived. The poem formally attempts to resurrect his memory but cannot sustain it.

abs-irish-nationalism.note: Nationalism is formally the absent ideal that structures the debate. The canvassers invoke nationalist principles but act pragmatically, formally showing the corruption of the ideal.

abs-working-class-representation.note: Working-class representation is formally the absent ideal championed by Hynes. Its absence formally shows the victory of pragmatism and class interest over principle.

abs-jacks-son-reform.note: The son's reform is formally absent and unlikely. Jack's lament formally shows the failure of education and discipline to produce virtue.

abs-economic-benefit.note: Economic benefit is formally the pragmatic concern that undermines ideological principle. Henchy's focus on economic advantage formally shows how material interest corrupts political discourse.
